issues.title: Malformed subdifferential definition

failure_location.quote:
For a convex function $\phi:\R^d\rightarrow (-\infty,\infty]$ we define the subdifferential as the (possibly empty) set
\[
\partial \phi(x) = \left\{y\in\R^d\;\middle|\; \forall h\in\R^d:\; \phi(x)+\langle y, x+h\rangle\leq \phi(x+h)\right\}.
\]

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Thus, $U(x)$ admits a minimizer which we can assume to be at $x=0$ without loss of generality.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the subdifferential is defined by φ(x)+⟨y,x+h⟩≤φ(x+h). Setting h=-x makes this require φ(x)≤φ(0), independently of y; for a strongly convex function minimized at zero, the displayed set is therefore empty whenever x≠0. The paper's SDE, explicit scheme, proximal identities, and subgradient inequalities instead require the standard condition φ(x)+⟨y,h⟩≤φ(x+h).
issues.overall_effect: Taken literally, the defined subdifferential does not supply the drift and optimality relations used throughout the continuous and explicit analyses and in several semi-implicit proofs. The intended standard reading restores those interfaces.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the defining inequality φ(x)+⟨y,x+h⟩≤φ(x+h) by the standard inequality φ(x)+⟨y,h⟩≤φ(x+h). All later occurrences of the subdifferential then retain their existing interpretation and require no proof changes.
issues.why_classification: The correction is uniquely forced by the old source’s proximal identity, SDE drift, and subsequent subgradient inequalities, all of which use the standard subdifferential. The erroneous extra x is never used mathematically, so an intended reader can correct this transcriptional defect and continue despite the large number of downstream locators.

issues.title: Invalid norm inference in the SDE moment proof

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $\tilde{X}^-_t\leq X_t\leq \tilde{X}^+_t$, for all $t$ component-wise almost surely.

issues.failure_explanation: From vectors a≤x≤b componentwise one cannot infer ||x||≤max{||a||,||b||}; for example, a=(-1,0), x=(-1,1), and b=(0,1) satisfy the componentwise order but ||x||=sqrt(2)>1. Thus the displayed inference does not establish the theorem's supremum second-moment clause. The valid consequence is ||X_t||^2≤||tilde X_t^-||^2+||tilde X_t^+||^2.
issues.overall_effect: The existence and uniqueness part has already been argued before the bad line, but the finite supremum second moment—and the later moment-continuity and contraction chain relying on it—is not established by the written proof.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the invalid maximum-norm inference by the componentwise consequence ||X_s||²≤||X̃_s^-||²+||X̃_s^+||². Taking the supremum over s and then expectations proves the stated finite supremum second moment and restores each dependent moment and contraction argument.
issues.why_classification: The proof makes a genuinely invalid inference, so the defect is not merely typographical. Its replacement is an elementary, local inequality that preserves every assumption, conclusion, rate, and downstream guarantee without a new lemma or substantive argument.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: the SDE \eqref{eq:sde} has a unique strong solution $(X_t)_{t \geq 0}$.

issues.title: Missing small-step qualifier in explicit-scheme ergodicity

failure_location.quote: The Markov chain $(X^\tau_k)_{k \in \N}$ from \eqref{eq:explicit_scheme} with $X_0^\tau=x_0\in\R^d$ arbitrary is geometrically ergodic.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where the last inequality holds for $\tau$ sufficiently small.

issues.failure_explanation: The proposition claims geometric ergodicity for every fixed τ>0, whereas its drift argument only works for sufficiently small τ. Under Ass:Potentials, U(x)=m x^2/2 is admissible and the update is X_{k+1}=(1-mτ)X_k+sqrt(2τ)W_k. At τ=2/m its variance grows linearly, and for τ>2/m the multiplier has magnitude greater than one, so the chain cannot converge geometrically to an invariant distribution.
issues.overall_effect: The unrestricted existence and geometric attraction of π^τ, and hence the unrestricted LLN claim that invokes this ergodicity result, fail for large steps. The small-step and vanishing-step conclusions remain available.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Introduce a constant τ₀>0 satisfying the bounds required in the displayed drift estimate and state both geometric ergodicity and the dependent LLN only for 0<τ≤τ₀. The small-step and vanishing-step stationary-distribution conclusions can remain unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The quadratic example shows that the all-step guarantee fails on a substantial and natural parameter regime, so restricting τ is a meaningful change to the algorithmic contract rather than a no-loss minor qualification. The existing drift proof already establishes the same ergodicity and LLN chain for sufficiently small steps, however, so the repair is contained and the surviving results are recognizably comparable.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Then, for $\tau>0$ sufficiently small, $(X_k^\tau)_k$ is geometrically ergodic

issues.title: Inconsistent step symbol in the semi-implicit update
issues.failure_explanation: The construction declares a constant step τ in the implicit inclusion, proximal parameter, and noise variance, but the purportedly equivalent executable update multiplies ∇F(X_k) by τ_k. Without an added definition τ_k=τ, this specifies a different or undefined parameter map.
issues.overall_effect: The displayed algorithm is internally inconsistent and does not unambiguously denote the constant-step chain analyzed by all subsequent semi-implicit results.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace τ_k multiplying ∇F(X_k) in the proximal update by the constant τ. This makes the executable update exactly equivalent to the preceding inclusion and leaves all dependent semi-implicit results unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The constant τ is uniquely forced by the preceding equation, the proximal parameter τG, the noise variance 2τ, and every subsequent analysis. No inference or construction must be changed beyond removing the unintended subscript.

issues.title: False all-step semi-implicit ergodicity and contraction

failure_location.quote: The proximal-gradient scheme with constant step size $\tau>0$ is geometrically ergodic with respect to the Wasserstein-2 distance

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem claims geometric ergodicity for every τ>0. With G=0 and F(x)=m x^2/2, which satisfies Ass:F_G with L=m, the scheme is the AR(1) chain with multiplier 1-mτ and is not ergodic once |1-mτ|≥1. Independently, the old proof's condition τ^2<1/(m+L) does not justify discarding the residual gradient term, and its final contraction factor omits τ. The revised calculation retains all coefficients and makes the residual term nonpositive under 0<τ<2/(m+L).
issues.overall_effect: The old theorem, the unrestricted semi-implicit LLN, and the stated moment-bound proof are unsupported outside a stable step-size interval. The asymptotic stationary-distribution result only needs a sufficiently small interval and can survive the restriction.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the synchronous-coupling calculation to retain the τ-dependent coefficients, yielding a contraction for 0<τ<2/(m+L). State the ergodicity and dependent LLN under that interval, and state the uniform moment bound for any τ_max<2/(m+L), using the resulting contraction/drift recursion.
issues.why_classification: The unrestricted theorem is false even for a quadratic F, and the old proof both uses an incorrect step condition and drops τ from the contraction factor. Repairing the full affected chain requires a contained but substantive recalculation and restricts a meaningful step-size regime, so it exceeds minor severity. The same semi-implicit algorithm, geometric ergodicity, LLN, moment control, and vanishing-step application survive on the standard stability interval without global proof reconstruction or major mathematical loss.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Then, the proximal-gradient scheme with constant step size $0<\tau<\tfrac{2}{m+L}$ is geometrically ergodic with respect to the Wasserstein-$2$ distance

issues.title: Belief-propagation TV applicability is reversed

failure_location.quote: While the presented methods would also work for the favorable isotropic TV functional, we will also compare the results to the ones obtained using Belief Propagation (BP) \cite[]{tapfre03,knobelreiter2020belief,narnhofer2022posterior} which is only applicable in the isotropic case.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In both cases, we define $G$ as the total variation functional \cite[]{rudin1992tv_mh}, $G(x) = \theta \TV(x)$ with $\theta>0$ a regularization parameter and $\TV(x)$ the anisotropic total variation
As a \emph{ground truth} to compare to, we employ the BP algorithm

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that BP is applicable only in the isotropic case. The same section explicitly defines the potentials used in both imaging examples with anisotropic TV and then says BP is employed as the comparison ground truth. If the old scope sentence were true, that declared comparison could not be performed on the declared target; changing the clause to anisotropic resolves the material inconsistency.
issues.overall_effect: The comparator's stated applicability is incompatible with the experimental target, making the BP comparison misleading as written, although no formal theorem is affected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace “only applicable in the isotropic case” by “only applicable in the anisotropic case,” leaving the explicitly defined anisotropic-TV targets and the BP comparisons unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The old source explicitly defines anisotropic TV in both experiments and then actually employs BP on those targets; together with the contrast to the alternative isotropic functional, this uniquely forces the corrected adjective. The reversal is transcriptional and requires no change to the experimental construction or any mathematical inference.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: which is only applicable in the anisotropic case.
